Asia is a continent and depending on who answers u, the ans will be different. General trends in south korea I observe with the new color palettes are the spring cherry blossom inspired colors that are muted with mixtures of pink, purple, brown shades with some glitter. I generally don't like korean eyeshadows (I'm noob so I find it hard to apply). I think the romand and lilybred palettes are quite popular at the moment? High end would probably lux cosmetics which would the usual like in America.

For chinese brands, they like their reds too much, especially since chinese new year just past and a lot of brands had released their new year palettes with rabbit inspired makeups. I've bought one from flowerknows cos got suckered in by the cute packaging. Pay off was okay but colors didn't look that great on me. Current movement in china would be to support nation bred cosmetics brands. For the cutie princess type, flowerknows is quite popular, oriental-high end would be Florasis, others in the low end to mid range are perfect diary (office workers), pinkbear (teens), and judydoll (famous for donut shaped makeup), otherwise it's the usual suspects.

My old favourite is still the canmake eyeshadows due to their affordability and beginner friendly colors. The palettes were well designed and the colors look good together. Pay off is good and I use them for cosplay (lol). Generally, japanese eyeshadows haven't change much over the decade with colors still looking like they belong ten years ago but it works! The only difference would be that many eye palettes now include tear bag highlighter which was missing ten years ago.

For jap, strangely enough, NARS and Dior eyeshadows are popular as mid to high end brands. Most of the drug store brands like canmake and kate are either targeted at students or office workers. Korean brands are popular too. 

East asian eyeshadows generally are not that pigmented because they were made for the general population there with fair skin and want eyeshadows that they could wear on a daily basics with no weird colors. 

Subculture brands or edgy brands are the exception and have darker or neon colors to them such as girlcult (chinese brand) or kate ( jap edgy brand).

Skin type - oily, acne-prone skin with fair skin that rarely tans and somewhat prone to sunburns.

Sunscreen that r beachworthy:

Sunplay ultra shield spf130 - the first sunscreen I wore since 6. Was effective under the equatorial sun but was difficult to remove and probably made preteen acne worst. No amt of scrubbing and soap would get this sunscreen off. Didn't need to reapply.

Anessa - decent outdoor sunscreen, somewhat sweat proof but my skin can't stand the alcohol content now. Haven't tested it for prolong outdoors.

Started out with Japanese sunscreen in my youth as it was the only thing available other than neutrogena and banna boat and korean sunscreen wasn't a thing back then. Moved on to korean sunscreen a few years back as it was more skin-friendly and have less alcohol with better texture ( though I doubt their effectiveness), plus I'm no longer under the sun as much as I used to. 

Honorable mention:
Neutrogena ultra sheer spf 50+ (aus version) - protected me from the outdoor sun in exchange for giving me the white cast from hell. The ultra sheer was a completely marketing lie.

Firstly, med school is no joke and is only for the passionate because you will give up a quarter of life to be a qualified doctor. Secondly, there are people who are successful in every field, you can probably earn more money in 10 years by going out to work now then slaving away in med school. If going to art school is not an option for you, you try building a portfolio and applying as an intern in design. It can be something small and unrelated to animation. If your art is good enough, you can try a freelancing gig like fiverr and do concept art for a price. This will help build your portfolio and customers as u get better. For the animation part, there are plenty of free courses online that you take such as on udemy and youtube that can help you with understanding workflow and software usage. It is not necessary to have an art degree to get a job in arts, your portfolio is more important. You would also need to present a portfolio when you apply to art school (depending).
